Please review the following manuscript written by my collaborator.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b09/review-experiment-f_i1mmah/call-1de7c7dd844d432e9a151198078647fd/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'ls -l manuscript.pdf; command -v pdftotext; command -v pdftoppm; command -v pdfinfo; command -v python3'

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs
python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(reader.pages))
print('Metadata:',reader.metadata)
parts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(reader.pages, 1):
    text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    parts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[:3]))
PY"

from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
parts=['\\n\\n===== PAGE '+str(i+1)+' =====\\n'+p.extract_text() for i,p in enumerate(r.pages)]
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript_plain.txt').write_text(''.join(parts))
print(''.join(parts[3:7]))
PY"

strengths: FedJETs addresses a useful problem: adapting predictions to unseen federated clients without labeled fine-tuning. Combining client-level expert downloads with per-sample routing is a coherent, potentially practical design.
The reported results are promising: Table 1 gives 95.7% accuracy on CIFAR10 and 78.6% on CIFAR100; initializing experts from the pretrained model raises CIFAR100 accuracy to 83.27% in Table 2.

Useful ablations examine pretrained-model quality, expert initialization, and anchor sampling. The appendix also considers overlapping label distributions and changing client populations. Reporting failure regimes provides valuable information.
The protocol diagram, loss functions, pseudocode, and optimizer settings make the core algorithm reasonably understandable.
weaknesses: Baseline validation is the principal obstacle to acceptance. On CIFAR10, FedAvg and FedProx initialized from the 93% checkpoint finish at 58.4% and 71.4%, while SCAFFOLD collapses to chance. Appendix B.1 acknowledges learning-rate inconsistency, but tuning ranges and validation procedures are unspecified. These failures require stronger investigation before supporting state-of-the-art claims. Against the listed frozen 93% model, FedJETs improves by 2.7 percentage points.

The main setup constructs anchors from disjoint label groups and allocates half of each round to them. The overlapping-label experiments partially relax this assumption, but the paper does not explain how suitable anchors would be identified in an existing federated population or evaluate unreliable anchor availability. Experiments remain limited to synthetic CIFAR label partitions, restricting the demonstrated generality.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism or establish efficiency. Table 1 uses five or ten experts for FedJETs versus two for FedMix. Figure 5 changes client sampling rather than directly ablating learned routing; Appendix F matches expert counts but sets M = K, removing sparsity. Comparisons holding capacity and anchor exposure fixed are needed. Communication volume, runtime, memory, and scaling are not measured, including the common feature extractor's costs.

Reproducibility and statistical support are insufficient. The manuscript provides no code link or independent-run uncertainty estimates, and omits important details of pretraining, data separation, gating-network dimensions, and baseline hyperparameters. Several appendix tables report the best test accuracy across evaluation rounds without specifying validation-based checkpoint selection.

The relationship to prior personalized and mixture-based federated learning is incomplete. Approaches such as FedEM explicitly model clients as mixtures of shared distributions and deserve substantive comparison. Appendix H's K-means visualization does not establish that learned clustering or mixture approaches are unsuitable, leaving the novelty beyond existing federated MoE methods insufficiently established.

Some central claims exceed their supporting analysis. Section 4 claims near-perfect expert selection, but Table 4 reports 27.1% error on CIFAR100 without clearly defining correct routing or separating routing error from classification error. Testing also aggregates the full unlabeled client dataset before selecting experts; the access assumption and performance with small incoming batches need clarification.

The claim of operating without violating data privacy is unsupported as stated. Keeping raw examples local does not establish privacy when expert identities and model updates are communicated. The claim should be scoped to local data retention unless stronger protection is substantiated.
